units.label: HAP-E 语料库的人机写作风格比较（主分析）
units.description: HAP-E作为主要语料的分析家族；共享人类首段提示和第二段对照，涵盖特征率、词汇和来源分类等分析。它与U005—U007有父级/子分析关系，不把这些条目简单相加为独立实验数。保留8,290个全部六模型均有输出的来源文本对应，含66,320块（每对应2个人类块和6个LLM块）。

units.label: CAP（COCA AI Parallel）语料库
units.description: 从 COCA（逾10亿词、八个语域）取样构造的第二平行语料，用于检验 HAP-E 结果的泛化性；n=9,615 文本对应，共 76,920 块（含人工 2 块与 6 个 LLM 输出）。

units.label: LLM 文本生成（六模型提示续写）
units.description: 以相同人类首段作为上下文/风格样例，调用GPT-4o、GPT-4o Mini及Llama 3的8B、70B、8B Instruct、70B Instruct续写，形成六种模型条件。主文未报告自行训练这些生成LLM；分析分类器的训练另记于U005。

units.label: Biber 语言特征提取（pseudobibeR / 66 特征）
units.description: 论文采用Biber 66类标签，使用R包pseudobibeR对依存解析文本计数；SI描述频率按每千词归一化，统计段和Table S5则使用tokens措辞。SI Table S4含平均词长（字符数，排除标点）和type-token ratio（含标点）等非普通频数指标。公开分类与效应量代码显式排除f_43_type_token；因此不能把作者所称66类直接当作每一分析的实用特征数，也不能把平均词长再按每千词归一化。

units.label: 来源分类分析：七类随机森林与二分类RF/lasso比较
units.description: 分析性学习组件：HAP-E七类随机森林；人类vs单一LLM的随机森林及lasso逻辑回归比较；HAP-E/CAP跨语料测试和M4迁移测试。共用特征/语料，不按每模型训练分别增加独立行为实验数。

units.label: 特征使用率与效应量比较（配对 Wilcoxon + Cohen's d）
units.description: 配对特征率、相对人类比率、signed-rank检验、图示90比较Bonferroni与paired d；具体公式及使用范围见F006/F022。

units.label: 词频比较（每百万词/每千词使用率）
units.description: lemma词频及作者报告的文本覆盖比例；语料汇总与文档覆盖两个单位分开，文字/代码冲突见I007。

units.label: M4 arXiv 摘要语料泛化检验
units.description: 使用 M4 平行语料的 arXiv 预印本摘要及 GPT-3.5 依据标题生成的摘要，作为不同 LLM、不同文类的泛化检查，用成对随机森林对其分类。

facts.statement: 研究问题是 LLM 的写作风格能否匹配人类，以及人类与不同 LLM 之间是否存在系统性的词汇、语法、修辞差异。作者原词包括 rhetorical styles、stylistic variation；任务是在相同人类文本首段条件下续写，语境涵盖多种英文文类。分析采用66类 Biber 特征，并另做词汇使用率比较。

method_function.text: 将文体比较的问题、续写任务和文类语境分开，保留作者报告的特征分析与词汇分析。

facts.statement: HAP-E来自学术、新闻、小说、口语、博客、影视剧本六类；CAP来自COCA八个语域，各初取12,000篇。SI明确CAP先筛约1,250词以上文本，再每语域随机抽1,500篇。HAP-E来源为Elsevier开放学术文、美国新闻站、Gutenberg小说、播客转写、blogger.com及影视脚本（部分OCR）；未明确其逐类初始配额。COCA每200词移除10词，作者因此另建HAP-E以缓解缺词对解析和特征提取的影响。

method_function.text: 提供跨文类/语域的人类文本作为平行比较基础。

facts.statement: 每篇取不跨章节边界的前约1,000词，用spaCy句界切成两个约500词块，以第一块为上下文、人类第二块为对照。SI明确指令模型用相同style/tone/diction续写500词的提示，基座Llama仅输入第一块；这两个条件的提示形式不同。每模型每来源在最终语料中保留一个续写，不能据此推断总调用、重试或额外采样次数。完整指令原文保存在E036。

method_function.text: 构造平行人机文本：同一提示下每个模型续写一份与第二个人类块对照。

facts.statement: 按SI删除含任一模型无响应或无意义输出的来源文本，另明确删除少于100词的响应；最终保留全部六模型都有有效输出的配对来源。HAP-E为8,290来源、66,320块；CAP为9,615来源、76,920块，每来源2个人类块加6个模型块。该共同有效样本筛选会影响最终语料组成，不能视为六模型独立抽样。

method_function.text: 记录拒答/短输出排除及共同有效样本条件；这不自动证明排除不会造成选择偏差。

facts.statement: 论文采用Biber 66类标签，使用R包pseudobibeR对依存解析文本计数；SI描述频率按每千词归一化，统计段和Table S5则使用tokens措辞。SI Table S4含平均词长（字符数，排除标点）和type-token ratio（含标点）等非普通频数指标。公开分类与效应量代码显式排除f_43_type_token；因此不能把作者所称66类直接当作每一分析的实用特征数，也不能把平均词长再按每千词归一化。

method_function.text: 提供可量化、可统计比较的语言特征集合。

facts.statement: 各模型与同来源人类chunk 2比较，使用配对Wilcoxon符号秩检验。Fig.3横轴为相对人类使用率（人类=1，对数刻度），纵轴为前15个重要特征。代码先按来源求逐文本特征均值，再除以人类chunk 2均值；图示显著性采用15×6=90的Bonferroni因子，阈值0.05。不能外推为对所有66类及全部分析统一使用该校正范围。

method_function.text: 统计检验人机特征使用率差异的显著性。

facts.statement: 作者报告：四个指令微调模型均偏好现在分词从句、作主语的‘that’从句、名物化与短语并列等信息密集、名词化特征。例如 GPT-4o 的现在分词从句使用率为人类的 5.3 倍（paired Cohen's d=1.38），作主语‘that’从句 2.6 倍（d=0.77），名物化 2.1 倍（d=1.23），短语并列 1.9 倍（d=0.81）。

method_function.text: 以使用率倍数与效应量描述人机风格差异方向与大小。

facts.statement: 七类来源随机森林（人类 chunk 2 与六个 LLM）在 HAP-E 测试集上的准确率为 66%，随机猜测期望为 14%；错分主要发生在同一模型不同规模/版本之间（Llama 8B 与 70B、两个 Instruct、GPT-4o 与 4o Mini），仅 4.2% 的 LLM 文本被误判为人类、9.8% 人类文本被误判为 LLM。测试集占 HAP-E 的 25%，含 n=14,535 条文本。

method_function.text: 用分类准确率与混淆矩阵评估特征可分性与误差结构。

facts.statement: 作者训练人类vs单一LLM的随机森林及lasso逻辑回归。主文概括RF通常93–98%、基座Llama的lasso约75%；需区分HAP-E内部测试与HAP-E/CAP交叉语料结果。SI Table S9的Training是袋外估计，Test列为另一语料；Table S10的Training经代码核查为拟合数据上的预测准确率，不能等同交叉验证准确率。SI给出ranger默认设置，lasso以10折交叉验证选一标准误惩罚。

method_function.text: 以成对分类与两种分类器比较可分性及特征交互作用。

facts.statement: 将各二分类随机森林应用于M4语料时，作者报告准确率下降：从指令微调LLM文本学得的分类器区分M4中GPT-3.5输出时高于随机水平；从Llama基座输出学得的分类器约50%。

method_function.text: 用外部语料检验分类器泛化性。

facts.statement: 词汇分析以HAP-E人类chunk 2为基准，原文说高于每百万词1次；公开代码用每千词率>=0.001（含边界）。代码将lemma小写、排除PUNCT及不含字母的项，按来源汇总lemma次数，再除以该来源过滤后的总词条数×1000。这是语料汇总词频，不是先逐篇归一化再平均。Fig.4横轴人类、纵轴LLM，均为对数尺度。

method_function.text: 以词频相对倍数刻画词汇过度使用。

facts.statement: 作者报告tapestry出现在23%的GPT-4o输出、amidst出现在27%；另在脚注指出词汇过度使用可能受生成伪影影响：Llama Instruct有时生成“Here is the continuation...”这类前缀；Llama 3 8B对Deborah的52倍使用率主要受一篇重复该词308次的输出影响。脚注没有证明前述tapestry/amidst比例也由同一伪影造成。 这些是作者报告的文本覆盖比例；公开代码对应实现存在计数单位冲突（见I007），本次未重算这些比例。

method_function.text: 以文档出现比例与词频倍数描述词汇偏差并标注伪影风险。

facts.statement: 已实施HAP-E/CAP双向跨语料分类与M4外部测试。SI明确HAP-E内部训练/测试为75%/25%并按文类分层；lasso代码按原始doc_id与genre分配10折后映回成对文本。随机森林内部切分代码未能清楚证实同来源各版本被成组隔离，跨语料RF还保留doc_id进入source~.的潜在实现问题；这些单列限制，不称已经验证无泄漏。

method_function.text: 通过跨语料与跨 LLM 检验结果稳健性。

facts.statement: 作者据Llama基座与Instruct版本的比较，提出instruction tuning可能解释文体偏离人类的现象。对GPT与Llama Instruct的差异，作者提出调优任务或偏好差异等可能解释，但承认缺少未调优GPT版本，且instruction tuning过程未公开，无法更精确确定原因。此处作为作者解释保存。

method_function.text: 以基座/指令微调对照解释风格差异来源。

facts.statement: 作者称 Biber 标签集在建模与分类文本上“significant success”，认为语言学视角可揭示区分机器生成文本的隐性信息，但明确表示其意图并非提出新的 LLM 检测器或用于监管学生写作。

method_function.text: 解释特征集与分类结果的价值边界。

facts.statement: 已检查主文7页、期刊SI22页及作者OSF代码的相关流程。提示、<100词排除、特征率聚合、配对效应量、RF/lasso配置已有证据；精确生成参数/重试、pseudobibeR与解析器实验版本仍未报告于核查材料。保留代码与文字的计数/特征集/验证范围差异；未执行作者代码、未复算论文结果。已核实的未知与冲突详见I001–I008。

method_function.text: 指出现有方法信息缺口对可复现性与解释的影响。

facts.statement: 六个被比较的生成模型为GPT-4o、GPT-4o Mini、Llama 3 8B、70B、8B Instruct和70B Instruct。主文描述调用这些模型生成文本；并未描述研究者为该实验训练这些生成LLM。该主文报告范围不等于证明所有分析步骤均无训练。 SI列出GPT-4o Mini版本2024-07-18、GPT-4o版本2024-08-06；GPT经Batch API默认设置生成，Llama经本地GPU的vLLM 0.5.5生成。缺失参数不以当前服务默认值补写。

method_function.text: 保留理解该方法及其解释边界所需的信息。

facts.statement: M4中使用的是arXiv人类摘要及GPT-3.5按预印本标题生成的摘要。

method_function.text: 保留理解该方法及其解释边界所需的信息。

facts.statement: 作者根据lasso逻辑回归只含加性项、而随机森林对Llama基座输出分类更好，推断Biber特征交互携带信息；此处记录作者基于模型比较所作的解释。

method_function.text: 保留理解该方法及其解释边界所需的信息。

facts.statement: 作者报告较大模型通常呈现与同系列较小模型相似的文体差异；基座Llama的特征使用率整体更接近人类。

method_function.text: 保留理解该方法及其解释边界所需的信息。

facts.statement: 提取者根据两个任务的材料对比：M4同时改变生成模型和文类/提示任务，不能从该测试单独识别哪一因素导致性能下降；它仍然是已实施的外部泛化检查。

method_function.text: 限制迁移性能下降的归因范围，同时保留实际泛化性验证。

facts.statement: 配对效应量按每个来源文本计算LLM特征率减人类chunk 2特征率，以差值均值除以差值标准差；SI与代码一致。Fig.S1绘制逐对差值除以该特征配对差值标准差后的分布；它不是均值效应量的置信区间。

method_function.text: 保留可复查的方法规则及适用范围，供后续方法归类使用。

facts.statement: 公开lasso代码在每个语料内对唯一doc_id/genre按文类分配10折，随机种子38；同来源的human/LLM记录继承同一foldid。cv.glmnet使用alpha=1、family=binomial；预测选lambda.1se。代码先用HAP-E拟合并测CAP，再反向重复。只将此分组保护归给lasso调参，不外推到所有RF切分。

method_function.text: 保留可复查的方法规则及适用范围，供后续方法归类使用。

facts.statement: 七类随机森林代码明确probability=TRUE和importance="impurity"，最大预测概率决定类别，以预测等于真实来源的比例计准确率；特征重要性用于选前15项作图。SI对ranger“默认设置”的概述不能覆盖代码中这两项显式选项。

method_function.text: 保留可复查的方法规则及适用范围，供后续方法归类使用。

facts.statement: 静态代码核查区分“作者报告的方法”与“发布实现”：RF跨语料表的训练列使用1-prediction.error；lasso训练列使用拟合数据预测；词汇的文本覆盖率实现用词条行数除以文档数，未按lemma×doc_id去重。这些实现证据不能证明它们就是生成出版结果的唯一版本；本次不复算，也不替作者修正结果。

method_function.text: 保留可复查的方法规则及适用范围，供后续方法归类使用。

facts.statement: 作者发布的classify-all代码还包含按前1–20重要特征拟合分类器的探索，以及把来源合并成人类/基座/指令模型三类的RF分析代码。主文与SI未提供其独立正式结果；仅记录代码存在，不推断实际执行或增加独立行为实验分母。

evidence.quote: from each text we extracted two consecutive chunks of roughly 500 words (split at sentence boundaries). The first chunk was provided to each LLM to give it context and a sample of the writing style. The LLMs were prompted to write 500 more words in the same style, tone, and diction;

text was then compared to the next 500-word chunk of the human text. We used six LLMs: GPT-4o and GPT-4o Mini (21, 22) and Meta Llama 3 8B, 70B, 8B Instruct, and 70B Instruct (23), producing six LLM-authored texts for each human-authored text.

We constructed the first corpus, the Human-AI Parallel English corpus, from six categories of text (academic, news, fiction, spoken word, blogs, and TV/movie scripts). The second corpus, the COCA AI Parallel (CAP) Corpus, is drawn from the pre-existing Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA), a large, representative corpus of over 1 billion words in eight registers: spoken, fiction, magazines, newspapers, academic, blogs, web pages, and TV/movie subtitles (24). The HAP-E corpus was used for our primary analyses, while CAP was used to evaluate the generalizability of the results to different texts.

The LLMs sometimes refused to respond to prompts or gave short, unusable answers; after these were removed, there were n = 8, 290 HAP-E texts and n = 9, 615 CAP texts with outputs from all LLMs. With two human chunks and six LLM-authored chunks for each text, HAP-E comprised n = 66, 320 chunks and CAP n = 76, 920 chunks.
As the instruction tuning processes are not publicly documented, it is not possible to determine the cause more precisely.)
We created two corpora of parallel human- and LLM-written texts. Each corpus began with n = 12, 000 human-authored English texts from a range of genres

To extract meaningful features from our corpus for training our classifiers, we used Douglas Biber’s tagset of 66 linguistic categories (19, 25, 26), which includes indices of lexical complexity and raw linguistic features ranging from the lexical to the grammatical.
Differences between LLM and human use of features were tested for statistical significance with the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Bonferroni multiple comparison correction.

For example, GPT-4o uses present participial clauses at 5.3 times the rate of humans (paired Cohen’s d = 1.38), ‘that’ clauses as subject 2.6 times as often (d = 0.77), nominalizations 2.1 times as often (d = 1.23), and phrasal coordination 1.9 times as often (d = 0.81).

Also, instruction tuning appears to make the model output less human, not more: the Llama 3 base models use features at rates similar to human texts, while GPT-4o and Llama 3 instruction-tuned models have much wider variation from feature to feature.

Classifying text by source. A random forest classifier using the Biber features to distinguish between the seven text sources in HAP-E (human chunk 2 and the six LLMs) achieved a test accuracy of 66%, compared to an expected accuracy of 14% from random guessing.
Overall, only 4.2% of LLM texts were falsely classified as human, and only 9.8% of human texts were falsely classified as LLMs.

A third major finding of this work is significant success of Biber’s tagset in modeling and classifying text. This success suggests that varied linguistic perspectives—which, perhaps, are not prioritized during the development and in-house assessments of LLMs—can reveal otherwise tacit information that distinguishes a text as machine-generated. With the linguistic perspective offered by pseudobibeR, we built a model that recognizes machine-generated text with relative ease.

to detect LLM output, none has studied the rhetorical styles of LLMs. Using several variants of Llama 3 and GPT-4o, we construct two parallel corpora of human- and LLM-written texts from common prompts. Using Douglas Biber’s set of lexical, grammatical, and rhetorical features, we identify systematic differences between LLMs and humans and between different LLMs. These differences persist when moving from smaller models to larger ones, and are larger for instruction-tuned models than base models. This observation of differences demonstrates that despite their advanced abilities, LLMs struggle to match human stylistic variation. Attention to more advanced linguistic features can hence detect patterns in their behavior not previously recognized.

To extract meaningful features from our corpus for training our classifiers, we used Douglas Biber’s tagset of 66 linguistic categories (19, 25, 26), which includes indices of lexical complexity and raw linguistic features ranging from the lexical to the grammatical. For example, features include mean word length, the use of nominalizations (nouns formed from adjectives or verbs, such as development or robustness), agentless passive voice, hedging phrases (such as something like or almost), and clausal coordination. All features are listed in the SI Appendix, Table S4. Differences between LLM and human use of features were tested for statistical significance with the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Bonferroni multiple comparison correction.

Fig. 3. Rate of Biber feature use by different LLMs, relative to the human usage of each feature, for the top 15 most important features in the HAP-E corpus. Note the log scale. GPT-4o and GPT-4o Mini show the largest variation from human texts, while the base variants of Llama 3 most closely resemble human grammar and style. Larger models (top row) generally show the same stylistic differences as their smaller counterparts (bottom row), despite performing better on other benchmark tasks. Triangles indicate statistically significant differences from human usage. Figure S1 of the SI Appendix gives the distributions of paired differences.

Fig. 2. Confusion matrix for a random forest classifying HAP-E texts by their linguistic and rhetorical features, evaluated on the test set (25% of the HAP-E corpus, including n = 14, 535 human and LLM texts). The block diagonal structure indicates that most classification errors were between different versions of the same LLM, rather than between humans and LLMs.

Fig. 4. Rates of word use by different LLMs (per 1,000 words) compared to the human use of each word in chunk 2, in the HAP-E corpus (log scale). Includes all words used more than once per million words in chunk 2. Words are lemmatized to group together inflected forms. Words on the diagonal are used equally often in human and LLM texts. Dashed blue lines indicate the range between 10× more and 10× less than human use. Note that the instruction-tuned models show more variation from the diagonal, indicating more deviation in vocabulary use relative to humans.

Some overuse may be artifacts of the generation process; for example, Llama 3 instruction-tuned variants overuse continuation because their outputs sometimes begin with “Here is the continuation of the text...” Llama base models have a tendency to repeat themselves, so Llama 3 8B uses Deborah at 52 times the rate of humans largely because of a single document repeating it 308 times.

That said, our intention is not to propose another way to construct LLM detectors or to police the writing of students and learners. Instead, we maintain that this type of comparative analysis is useful for identifying differences between human- and machine-generated text, zeroing in on specific teachable moments in the revision of machinegenerated text.

As a further check of generalizability, we used part of the M4 parallel corpus (17) consisting of abstracts from the arXiv preprint service alongside abstracts generated by GPT-3.5 when prompted with the preprint title. These texts are from a different LLM (GPT-3.5) and a very distinct genre of writing (academic abstracts), providing a check on the consistency of results in different genres.

Typical accuracies achieved by random forests were 93–98% even when trained on HAP-E and tested on CAP or vice versa (SI Appendix Table S9). Lasso-penalized logistic regression classifiers attained similar performance for all LLMs except for the Llama base models, which had accuracies around 75% (SI Appendix Table S10). Since the lasso regressions only consider additive terms, this implies that interactions between the Biber features contain relevant signals for the Llama base models.

A second major finding of this research is the apparently central role of instruction tuning in creating these discrepancies between human and model general texts. While we do not have access to untuned versions of GPT, comparisons between Llama’s base and tuned models emphasize the degree to which instruction tuning pushes models to produce text that reads unlike a human. This suggests that differences in style are not simply due to the selection of texts for training the base models, but due to the instruction-tuning process. Similarly, differences between GPT-4o and the instructiontuned Llama variants may be due to differences in instruction tuning, either through different human preferences in rating responses or differences in the tasks (such as summarization) used to tune the models. (As the instruction tuning processes are not publicly documented, it is not possible to determine the cause more precisely.) While instruction tuning has

19         3. splitting each string into approximately 500-word chunks (with the split-point being a sentence boundary as

25    The resulting corpora, then, contain the first chunk of human-authored text (the “germinal” text used for the LLM
26    prompt) and seven variations of the second chunk: the original (human-authored) continuation of the first chunk, and
27    continuations generated by six different LLMs. This workflow is illustrated in Figure TODO of the main text. The
28    figure also highlights the alignment of the second, parallel chunks, which enable comparisons between the writing of
29    humans and LLMs, as well as comparisons among the writing produced by the LLMs, themselves.

30       The first of our parallel corpora uses the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) as the source
31    of its human-authored text and is called the COCA AI Parallel (CAP) corpus. As noted above, we wanted data
32    representative of a broad range of sources and registers. COCA is a monitor corpus with over 1 billion words and
33    balanced among eight registers: spoken, fiction, magazines, newspapers, academic journals, blogs, other web pages,
34    and TV/movie subtitles (2). For our dataset, we filtered for texts containing a minimum of approximately 1,250
35    words, then randomly sampled 1,500 documents from each register to create a corpus of 12,000 texts.
36       Though its breadth and representativeness make COCA valuable for this task, it does have a key limitation: to
37    allow distribution of otherwise copyrighted material, COCA alters the text by removing 10 words every 200 words.∗
38    This produces gaps and incomplete sentences in each 500-word chunk that might affect sentence parsing and feature
39    extraction. For this reason, we constructed a second corpus, which is meant to approximate COCA’s composition.
40       The resulting dataset, the Human AI Parallel English (HAP-E) corpus, is drawn from six (as opposed to COCA’s
41    eight) text-types:†

42         • Academic: samples were drawn from a 40,000+ document corpus of open-access academic articles published
43           by Elsevier.

44         • News: samples were drawn from a 100,000+ document corpus of news articles published online by U.S.-based
45           news organizations.

46         • Fiction: samples were drawn from novels and short stories in the public domain and available on Project
47           Gutenberg.

48         • Spoken: samples were drawn from a corpus of 100,000 podcast transcriptions. (Note that COCA’s spoken
49           text-type comes from transcriptions of unscripted news shows.)

50         • Blogs: samples were drawn from a corpus of 681,288 posts from blogger.com.

51         • Television and Movie Scripts: samples were drawn from two different corpora of scripts, some of which
52           were converted using OCR.

53    The sampling and processing of the HAP-E corpus followed the same five steps described at the beginning of this
54    section. The word counts of the HAP-E and CAP corpora can be found in the Appendix, Tables S2 and S3.

88        To tag the texts, we used the pseudobibeR package for R, which counts Biber features present in dependency-parsed
89     texts.‡ pseudobibeR has proven effective at reproducing results similar to those of other studies that use Biber’s
90     tagset (11, 12). Once tagged, we counted the rate of occurrence of each feature per 1,000 words of text. These rates
91     served as the features for our analysis.

101   Statistical analysis. To compare the rate of feature use between human and LLM texts, we compared each LLM’s
102   rate of use with the human chunk 2 usage. Table S5 shows the usage (per 1,000 tokens) of each feature in human
103   text, and the LLM usage scaled relative to the human usage of each feature. To scale these differences relative to
104   the typical variation in usage across texts, we calculated the difference between the LLM and human rates for each
105   individual text, then calculated the Cohen’s d effect size by dividing the mean difference by the standard deviation of
106   the differences. These effect sizes are shown in Table S6. Typically, d ≤ 0.5 is considered a small effect, 0.5 < d ≤ 0.8
107   is considered medium, 0.8 < d ≤ 1.3 is large, and d > 1.3 is very large (20). Differences were tested for significance
108   using the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

109   Classification. To evaluate whether the features described above are sufficient to distinguish between human- and
110   LLM-written text, we randomly split the HAP-E documents into a training set (75%) and a test set (25%), stratifying
111   by document category.
112      First, we fit a random forest to classify the source of each of the texts using the Biber features. This is a seven-class
113   classification task (human and six LLMs). This random forest identified the features most important for distinguishing
114   between sources; these top features are used for visualizations of feature variations by source. This was fit using the
115   ranger package (21) with its default settings.
116      Next, we trained a random forest for each pairwise human vs. LLM training task: human vs. GPT-4o, human
117   vs. Llama 3 8B, and so on. For comparison, we also fit lasso-penalized logistic regression models using the same set
118   of Biber features. We used the performance of the lasso models to benchmark and provide context to the random
119   forest models. Since we only account for linear additive contributions of the Biber features in the lasso models,
120   any noticeable improvements in performance of the random forests are due to the flexibility of tree-based models
121   in capturing the presence of non-linear interactions. All lasso logistic regression models were fit using the glmnet
122   package with the one-standard-error regularization penalty selected with 10-fold cross-validation (22). Accuracies of
123   the random forest and lasso models on the test set are shown in Tables S9 and S10.
124      Finally, we used these models to classify text from the M4 parallel corpus (7). We focus on its arXiv GPT-3.5
125   dataset, which includes both real abstracts of preprints posted on arXiv and text generated by GPT-3.5 when
126   prompted to write an abstract based on the preprint’s title. This provides an external test set, generated on a different
127   task with a different model, to evaluate the generalizability of our classifiers. The accuracies on this test set are
128   shown in Tables S11 and S12.

## Classifying humans vs. base vs. instruction-tuned

Let's reduce the data labels to just human vs. base vs. instruction-tuned LLMs, not by specific source.

### Fit a random forest

```{r base-instruct-human, cache=TRUE}
source_type <- function(source) {
  factor(case_when(
    is_human(source) ~ "human",
    is_instruct(source) ~ "instruct",
    .default = "base"))
}

is_human <- function(source) {
  source %in% c("Chunk 1", "Chunk 2")
}

is_instruct <- function(source) {
  startsWith(as.character(source), "GPT") |
    endsWith(as.character(source), "Instruct")
}


train_ai <- train |>
  mutate(source = source_type(source))

test_ai <- test |>
  mutate(source = source_type(source))

fit_ai <- ranger(source ~ ., data = train_ai, importance = "impurity",
                 probability = TRUE)

importances_ai <- data.frame(feature = names(importance(fit_ai)),
                             importance = importance(fit_ai))
```

### Get test accuracy

```{r}
test_accuracy(fit_ai, test_ai)
```

issues.description: 75/25文类分层已由SI确认；lasso成组调参由代码确认。RF内部代码nest(data=doc_id)后initial_split(strata=genre)，未明确按原始文档ID组切分；跨语料RF的doc_id保留后进入source~.，与仅用Biber特征的文字描述存在实现疑点。未运行数据，不能断言实际泄漏或其影响。
issues.impact: 后续不能把全流程编码为已验证成组隔离/纯Biber输入；文内留出、袋外、拟合数据和跨语料性能分列。

issues.description: 作者明确声明研究目的不是提出新的LLM检测器或监管学生写作；不能据此推出“没有外部验证”。实际CAP/M4泛化测试已报告。这里的不适用仅指将论文当成部署级检测器认证。
issues.checked_scope: P006 Discussion 中关于分类器用途的声明。
issues.impact: 把作者意图与实际验证流程分开；不删去已实施的泛化性评估。

issues.description: SI已描述pseudobibeR依存特征计数并列Table S4；OSF直接读取预计算Biber特征，未提供本次提取版本及完整parser/tagger生成脚本。文献中的工具有效性论述不等于本数据上实施了人工复核或标注准确率验证。
issues.checked_scope: SI第3、8–9页及OSF分析输入读取段；未读取当前最新工具源码来冒充历史实验版本。
issues.impact: 计数功能可交接；具体实现版本和本数据标注有效性保持未报告，不补造控制。

issues.description: 已核查SI全文及词频代码：未见删除生成前缀/重复词后重新估计效果的敏感性分析。作者另报告按包含词的文本比例观察极端词，但该实现有I007计数冲突，不能据此认定生成伪影已得到控制。
issues.checked_scope: 主文脚注、SI1–22页、vocab-compare预处理与相对词率/覆盖率段。
issues.impact: 保留伪影影响这一解释限制；不把风险讨论当作实际排除或验证。

issues.description: 配对d公式已核实。仍须保留计分范围差异：SI按每千words描述频数，表格写tokens，平均词长/TTR另有定义；代码显式排除TTR。预计算Biber数据的生成脚本不在此包，不能确认每种指标完整tokenization/归一化实现。
issues.impact: 后续可使用已确认公式和聚合层级；不得把全部66类一律解释为每千词频数。

issues.description: 论文/SI将tapestry等比例描述为含该词的文本占比，但vocab-compare 199–203行按source/lemma分组后n()/n_docs，未按文档去重；这是词条出现次数与文档覆盖率的单位冲突。不能把发布代码推断值当作重新验证的论文比例。
issues.checked_scope: 期刊XML关联、SI原PDF关键页、OSF发布元数据及相应代码静态核查。
issues.impact: 覆盖率式测量的实际实现不确定；作者报告值保留为报告结果，不作已验证计算。

issues.description: 取得的是期刊SI及2024年12月更新的OSF代码，冻结主文为arXiv v2；身份与主要样本/模型/效应一致，但不是已证明同一运行版本。SI Table S2有5550,463这一异常数字，视觉检查确认原文件如此；不据其自行改写样本或重算。
issues.checked_scope: 期刊XML关联、SI原PDF关键页、OSF发布元数据及相应代码静态核查。
issues.impact: 版本和排版异常显式保留；不将所有文字/代码拼接为一个已执行且无矛盾的实验。
